echoes.note: Luke dates the Troas voyage 'after the days of Unleavened Bread,' invoking the Passover/Massot calendar prescribed here. The festival reference is precise and structural (it anchors the chronology), though it functions as a time-marker rather than an interpretive citation; volume is moderate, recurrence in Luke-Acts of festal dating is real (cf. Pentecost in v.16).
Deuteronomy's restatement of the seven days of unleavened bread underlies the same festal marker; an alternative locus for the calendar allusion behind 'days of Unleavened Bread.'

The recurring 'plot made against him by Jews' (v.3, cf. v.19) resonates faintly with the lament topos of the righteous sufferer surrounded by those who scheme to take his life; thematic coherence with Paul-as-persecuted-servant, but no verbal borrowing.

The raising of Eutychus is a deliberate Elijah typology: a man of God descends to a dead youth, throws himself upon the body, and the boy's life returns. Elijah 'stretched himself upon the child' (LXX) and the child's life came back to him; Paul 'fell upon him, embracing him' and declares 'his life is in him.' Volume is high (the bodily prostration on the corpse), recurrence strong (Luke pairs his apostles with Elijah/Elisha resurrections elsewhere), thematic coherence excellent.

The Elisha raising of the Shunammite's son is the closest structural twin: prophet enters where the dead child lies, stretches/lies upon him, life returns, and the living child is restored to the household 'greatly comforted.' The deliverance of the boy 'alive' (v.12) mirrors the son given back. Two resurrection narratives converge here, reinforcing the Elijah/Elisha pattern.
The Shunammite boy's collapse and death by midday provides the death-of-the-youth setup that the raising narrative answers; included as the antecedent scene to the 2 Kings 4:32-37 type.

Paul hastens 'to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost' (v.16); the Feast of Weeks counted fifty days from the Massot offering is legislated here, naming and grounding the festival Luke invokes. The reference is precise but functions chronologically rather than as exegetical citation.
Deuteronomy's command to keep the Feast of Weeks at the place the Lord chooses (Jerusalem) underlies Paul's urgency to be there for Pentecost; an alternative locus for the festal allusion.

Paul's self-description as one who 'didn't shrink from declaring anything profitable' (v.20) and testified repentance (v.21) begins the watchman motif that crests in v.26-27; the prophet appointed watchman who must declare the whole message anticipates Paul's accounting. Verbal overlap is light here, fuller in the next pericope.

'I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem' (v.22) and the Spirit's testimony that 'bonds and afflictions wait for me' (v.23) resonate with the prophetic compulsion to a costly word one cannot withhold; thematic coherence with Jeremiah's constrained, suffering vocation, no verbal borrowing.

Paul's ministry 'with many tears' amid 'plots of the Jews' (v.19) and his journey toward inevitable suffering echoes the deuteronomistic pattern of the persistently rejected prophets/messengers; faint thematic link.

Paul's 'I am clean from the blood of all men' (v.26) directly takes up the watchman oracle: the watchman who warns is innocent of the blood of those who perish, while the negligent watchman bears their blood. The blood-guilt formula is distinctive and the watchman-over-the-people role frames the whole farewell. High volume and thematic coherence.

The first watchman commission, where the prophet who fails to warn has the sinner's blood 'required at your hand' but the faithful one 'delivers his soul,' is the twin source of Paul's blood-innocence claim (v.26) tied to declaring 'the whole counsel of God' (v.27). Recurs with Ezek 33; together a strong watchman intertext.

The charge to 'shepherd the assembly of the Lord' and guard 'all the flock' over which they are made overseers (v.28), against shepherds who exploit and fail to protect, draws on Ezekiel's oracle against the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and let the flock be scattered and devoured. The overseer-shepherd-flock cluster is dense and coherent.
The tender shepherd who gathers and feeds the flock informs the pastoral 'shepherd the assembly' charge (v.28); the positive shepherd image complements the Ezekiel 34 indictment.

'Vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock' (v.29) takes up Ezekiel's image of the princes 'like wolves tearing the prey, shedding blood, destroying souls' for gain. The wolves-versus-flock predation maps closely onto the corrupt leaders devouring the people.
Zephaniah's officials as 'evening wolves that leave nothing for the morning' is a strong alternative locus for the savage-wolves-not-sparing image (v.29); reinforces the prophetic wolf-leader topos.

The flock scattered and become food for 'every beast of the field' because there was no shepherd undergirds the warning that wolves will ravage the flock after Paul's departure (v.29); ties the wolf threat back into the Ezekiel 34 shepherd oracle.

'Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them' (v.30) echoes the Deuteronomic warning against prophets who arise from within Israel to lead the people astray after them, who must be purged; thematic and structural coherence (internal seducers drawing the people away).
The worthless shepherd who abandons and devours the flock provides a further wolf/false-shepherd resonance for the predatory leaders foreseen in v.29-30.

Moses' prayer for a successor 'that the congregation of the Lord be not as sheep without a shepherd' faintly underlies Paul's succession-anxiety farewell, handing the flock to the elders before his departure (v.28-31).

'The inheritance among all those who are sanctified' (v.32) echoes Moses' blessing where the holy ones are in God's hand and Moses commands the law as 'an inheritance' for the assembly; the sanctified-ones-plus-inheritance pairing is distinctive.

'His lot is among the saints' (the righteous numbered among the holy ones / sons of God) is a close deuterocanonical parallel to 'the inheritance among all those who are sanctified' (v.32); strong conceptual and lexical fit for the eschatological inheritance among the holy.

Paul's farewell protest 'I coveted no one's silver, or gold, or clothing' (v.33-34) closely mirrors Samuel's farewell self-vindication: 'Whose ox have I taken? ... from whose hand have I taken a bribe?' with the people as witnesses. Both are leaders' departure speeches asserting financial blamelessness; high structural and thematic coherence.

Moses' protest 'I have not taken one donkey from them, neither have I hurt one of them' is a second leader's disavowal of taking from the people, reinforcing Paul's 'I coveted no one's silver or gold' (v.33).

'It is more blessed to give than to receive' (v.35) coheres with the wisdom maxim that the one who scatters increases while the one who withholds comes to want, and the generous soul is enriched; OT sapiential ground for the generosity logion.
Sirach's exhortation to give to the poor and help the weak/needy is a deuterocanonical parallel to laboring 'to help the weak' and the blessedness of giving (v.35).

'They all wept a lot, and fell on Paul's neck and kissed him' (v.37) reproduces the Joseph reunion idiom: falling on the neck, weeping, and kissing. The verbal cluster (neck + weeping + kiss) is distinctive Septuagintal language for emotional parting/reunion.
Esau 'fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept' is a second close parallel for the falling-on-the-neck, weeping, kissing farewell of v.37.
Naomi's parting from her daughters-in-law, who 'lifted up their voices and wept' and 'kissed' at separation, offers a further departure-with-weeping-and-kissing resonance for v.37.
